title: Most from my students (Taanit 7a)
hookLine: Rabbi Chanina: much from my teachers, more from my friends, most of all from my students

cards: A grandmother gets a new phone, and her ten-year-old grandson shows her how to video call. Three minutes, and she's in. A manager asks the new intern a question just to be nice, and the answer changes the whole project.

A parent explains why the sky is blue, gets asked why five times, and realizes they never really understood it. Most people picture learning flowing one way, from older to younger, from expert to beginner.
The Talmud has a sage who said it runs the other way too, and most of all.

teach.b: In tractate Taanit, the rabbis ask why the Torah is compared to a tree. Proverbs says of wisdom: "She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her." Why a tree?

teach.h: A SMALL STICK LIGHTS A BIG LOG.
teach.b: One sage explains: just as a small stick can set a big log on fire, so younger students sharpen great scholars.
Then the Talmud quotes Rabbi Chanina: I have learned much from my teachers, and more from my friends, and from my students more than from all of them. Three circles.
One way to read it: teachers give you the most at the start, the foundation, the words, the method. Friends, study partners, push you further, because they argue back as equals.

teach.h: TEACHING SHOWS WHAT YOU DON'T KNOW.
teach.b: Students push you most of all, because teaching exposes what you don't know. A student asks the question you'd stopped asking. They see the text with fresh eyes, without your assumptions.
And you have to explain it so clearly that you finally understand it yourself. The same passage quotes another verse: iron sharpens iron. Two blades rubbing together, each making the other sharper.
That's the passage's picture: not a lecture, but sparks. And Rabbi Chanina's line is a kind of humility. Even the great sage, at the top of the ladder, says his best teachers were the ones below him.

how: Jewish study often pairs learners of different levels, and teachers commonly quote Rabbi Chanina's saying to honor what they learn from their students.

games.q: you're a great scholar. a young student asks a question you'd stopped asking years ago. what do you do?
o: give the standard answer and move on.
stop, think, and learn from the question.
tell them they'll understand when they're older.
games.why: Rabbi Chanina said he learned most of all from his students: a small stick can set a big log on fire.

practice: Think of someone younger or newer than you: a child, a niece, a new coworker, a beginner in your hobby. Remember something they asked or said that made you see something differently.
Then think of one question you could ask them, not to test them but to learn what they know that you don't, and picture really listening to the answer.
